board_events.text: Read a row across and you get three answers at once: how many membranes, which cells, and what it does.
The 'FOUND IN' column is the one students skip — and it is where CUET matching questions live.
Watch the narrow ones: PLASTID is plant cells and euglenoids. LYSOSOME is eukaryotes, especially animal.
And the broad ones: PLASMA MEMBRANE and RIBOSOME are found in ALL CELLS. Only those two.
Use it as a SELF-TEST: cover the right-hand column and reconstruct it. Then cover the left and work backwards.
That two-way drill is exactly what a matching question demands.

segments.text: Two decisions. And I want you to see them as decisions, not as categories, because that is what makes them stick. Life reached a fork, and both branches worked.
Look at the board. One cell at the top, splitting twice. The first split is universal. The second split only happens on one branch of the first. That structure matters.
Fork one is about how to handle the genetic material and the chemistry of the cell. Where do you put the D N A, and where do you run the reactions? Two answers were possible.

The prokaryote's answer: keep the D N A naked in the cytoplasm, in a region called the nucleoid, and run every reaction in one undivided space. And note the three adjectives the source gives it — fast, simple, ancient. Not primitive. Ancient, and still winning.

The eukaryote's answer: lock the D N A inside a membrane-bound nucleus, and parcel the chemistry into membrane-bound organelles. And the payoff is exactly what we saw in sub-topic two — incompatible processes run side by side without interfering.

So that single contrast, compartmentalised or not, organises the entire chapter. Every organelle you learned exists because of the eukaryotic answer. The mesosome exists because of the prokaryotic one.

Fork two is narrower. It is about how a eukaryote makes its living, and it only applies once you are already on the eukaryotic branch. The plant design: a rigid cellulose wall, plastids to capture light, and a giant water-filled vacuole for turgor.

The animal design: no wall, no plastids. But centrioles, and a flexible, mobile shape. Notice the trade — the plant bought stability and light-capture; the animal bought movement. Neither is better. They are different bets.
Now the compression. Everything we just said about two forks can be squeezed into a single question, and once you see it you cannot unsee it.
The chapter is really one question asked twice. And the question is this: what is walled off from what?
Look at the board. One question at the top, splitting into two. And notice both halves are literally the same words, applied to different things.
Prokaryote versus eukaryote asks: is the D N A walled off? A prokaryote says no — the D N A lies naked in the cytoplasm. A eukaryote says yes — there is an envelope around it.
Plant versus animal asks: is the whole cell walled off? A plant says yes — a rigid cellulose wall around the outside. An animal says no — just a membrane, flexible and bare.
So look at what changed between the two forks. Not the question. Only the scale. Fork one is a wall around the D N A. Fork two is a wall around the cell. Zoom in, or zoom out.

<excited>Same question, two scales. And answer those two and the organelles fall into place. Because once you know whether the D N A is walled off, you know whether there are organelles at all. And once you know whether the cell is walled off, you know whether there are plastids and a big vacuole and a fixed shape.
This is the compression to carry into the exam hall. Not a table. One sentence, that reorganises a whole chapter into something you can hold in your head while the clock runs.
Three cautions before the tables. Each one is a place where a clean statement we have been making needs a qualifier, and each qualifier is examinable.
Caution one is about the reach of fork two. The plant-animal contrast applies to eukaryotes only. It is meaningless for bacteria, and that is not a small technicality.

Think about why. Fork two is a question about what kind of eukaryote you are. A bacterium never took fork one's eukaryotic branch, so it never arrives at fork two at all. A bacterium is neither plant-like nor animal-like. It is off that road entirely.
Caution two is more subtle, and it is about honesty. We have been saying higher plants lack centrioles. That is the safe rule, and it is what the exam wants. But it is a convention, not an absolute.

The truth is that some lower plant cells do have them — specifically, the motile gametes of certain algae and bryophytes. And if you think about it, that makes complete sense: those gametes swim, swimming needs flagella, and flagella need basal bodies, which are centrioles.

<whisper>So how do you handle that in an exam? Stick to the higher-plant convention unless told otherwise. Notice the word higher is doing the work in the standard statement. The rule is not plants lack centrioles; it is higher plants lack centrioles. Learn the qualified version and you are safe either way.
Caution three is one you have met before, and it is worth repeating precisely because it is the oldest asterisk in the chapter.
Remember the cell theory's standing exception: viruses are acellular and fall outside it. Same answer as in sub-topic one. The theory is not wrong about viruses; it simply does not cover them.
Now the master comparison, and we take it in two halves for a reason. Some rows decide the question. Some rows only describe it. Mixing them up is how marks get lost.

Look at the board. Three gold rows, then two plain ones. The gold rows are the answer to what makes a eukaryote. The plain rows are strong supporting evidence, but they do not settle anything on their own.
Gold row one: the true nucleus. Absent in prokaryotes — the D N A lies in a nucleoid, which is a region, not a compartment. Present in eukaryotes — the D N A is enclosed by a nuclear envelope.
Gold row two: the nuclear membrane. Absent. Present, and be specific: double, with pores. Those two details, double and pores, are worth stating in full.

Gold row three: membrane-bound organelles. Absent. Present — E R, Golgi, mitochondria, and all the rest of sub-topic two. And notice rows one to three are really the same idea said three ways: is anything walled off inside?

Now the two supporting rows. Genetic material: a single, naked, circular D N A molecule plus plasmids, versus linear D N A wound on histones and packed into chromosomes. Naked and circular against wound and linear.

Ribosomes: seventy S, which is fifty S plus thirty S, versus eighty S in the cytoplasm. And do not drop the parenthesis — seventy S inside mitochondria and plastids. That bracket is where the marks hide.

<whisper>And now the sentence to write on the inside of your skull. The one criterion that never fails: a membrane-bound nucleus, and organelles, marks a eukaryote. Everything else — size, division rate, ribosome size — follows from that. If you are ever unsure which row settles a question, it is that one.

The second half of the table. These are the rows that follow from the architectural decision rather than constituting it, and they are still worth full marks in a board answer — they just cannot settle an argument.

Size first. Prokaryotes are generally smaller, roughly one to ten micrometres. Eukaryotes are generally larger, roughly ten to twenty, and up to a hundred. Note the word generally in both. These are ranges, not laws.
Now the cell wall row, and read it slowly because it catches people. Prokaryotes: peptidoglycan, if present at all. Eukaryotes: cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi, or absent in animals.

<curious>Did you notice what that row just did? It quietly demolished an assumption most students carry. Eukaryote does not mean no wall. Plants have walls. Fungi have walls. Only the animal cell has none. If you have been using wall as a prokaryote marker, stop — it does not work.

Organisation feature. The prokaryote's kit: mesosome, inclusion bodies, chromatophores. The eukaryote's kit: endomembrane system, cytoskeleton, nucleus. Read those two lists side by side and you are reading sub-topic one against sub-topics two and three.

Cell division: binary fission versus mitosis and meiosis. Simple split, versus the choreographed machinery you will meet in the next chapter. And notice the spindle needs a cytoskeleton — so even this row follows from the compartmentalisation decision.
Examples, worth memorising as a set. Prokaryotes: bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, P P L O. Eukaryotes: protists, fungi, plants, animals.

And the health warning on this whole table. These rows describe; they do not decide. If an option offers you size or division rate as the defining difference between the two groups, that option is wrong. It is offering you a symptom and calling it a cause.
The second master comparison, and the mistake students make here is starting from the differences. Start from the shared base instead, because it is much larger than the list of differences.
Both are eukaryotic. Which means both took fork one's compartmentalised branch, and both inherited everything that came with it.

So both have a true nucleus. Both have an endomembrane system. Both have mitochondria. Both have ribosomes. Both have a cytoskeleton. Look at the green band on the board — that is a lot of chapter sitting in the shared column.
And that reframes the question. They differ in a short, high-yield list. Short. Everything else is common ground, and the exam is only ever testing the short list.
So here is the clean way to remember what a plant cell adds. Three letters: W-P-V. Say them once and they stay.

W is wall, of cellulose. P is plastids, to capture light or to store. V is a big vacuole, maintaining turgor. Wall, plastids, vacuole. And notice each one is something the plant has and the animal simply does not.
<whisper>Now the reverse direction, because a good answer runs both ways. What does an animal cell uniquely keep? The centriole. One word. The plant gave it up; the animal held on to it.
So count what you just memorised. Four letters: W, P, V, and centriole. That is the core of a three-mark board question, and it fits on one line of rough paper.
Now the full table. Eight rows. And rather than memorise eight facts, I want you to see that most of them are one fact with consequences.

The first three you already have from W-P-V. Cell wall: present, of cellulose, versus absent. Plastids: present versus absent. Large central vacuole: present and maintaining turgor, versus absent or small.
Row four is the reverse fact. Centriole and centrosome: absent in higher plants, present in animals. Note the word higher is in the table itself — the convention is built into the source.

Row five: lysosomes. And this one is a nuance rather than a yes-or-no. Rare or less prominent in plants, common and prominent in animals. So do not write absent for plant lysosomes. Write rare. The table is being careful, and so should you.
Row six: plasmodesmata, present in plants as cytoplasmic bridges, absent in animals. You met these at the end of sub-topic two.
Row seven: stored carbohydrate. Starch versus glycogen. Two words, frequently asked, and easy marks if you have them ready.
Row eight: shape. Fixed in plants, because of the rigid wall. Variable and flexible in animals. And notice the table itself gives you the reason in brackets.

Row सात — stored carbohydrate. Starch बनाम glycogen. दो शब्द, अक्सर पूछे जाते हैं, और तैयार हों तो आसान marks.
Row आठ — shape. Plants में fixed, rigid wall की वजह से। Animals में variable और लचीला। और ध्यान दीजिए table ख़ुद brackets में वजह दे रहा है।

<curious>अब पीछे हटिए और पूरी list देखिए। Fixed shape — wall की वजह से। Plasmodesmata — दीवार में से channels तभी चाहिए जब दीवार हो। बड़ा vacuole — वो wall पर बाहर की तरफ़ दबाव डाल कर turgor बनाता है, जो बिना wall के बेमतलब है। आठ में से तीन rows एक ही फ़ैसले से निकलती हैं। Wall सिर्फ़ list पर दिखता नहीं; वो list को explain करता है।
पूरे chapter के लिए एक table. हर organelle जिससे आप मिले, एक पन्ने पर, तीन columns के साथ। यही वो consolidation है जिसके लिए ये sub-topic बना है।
देखिए इसे पढ़ना कैसे है। एक row आर-पार पढ़िए और आपको एक साथ तीन जवाब मिलते हैं। कितनी membranes. किन cells में मिलता है। और वो करता क्या है। हर row में तीन facts, तेरह rows.

अब वो column जो students छोड़ देते हैं। वो बीच वाला है — found in. हर कोई organelle और function सीखता है। लगभग कोई organelle और location की drill नहीं करता। और वही बीच वाला column ठीक वहाँ है जहाँ C U E T के matching सवाल रहते हैं।

तो संकरी entries पर ख़ास ध्यान दीजिए। Plastid — plant cells और euglenoids. सारे eukaryotes नहीं — plants और euglenoids. Lysosome — eukaryotes, ख़ास तौर पर animal. शब्द ख़ास तौर पर देखिए, वही सावधान काम करता हुआ जो पिछले table में rare कर रहा था।
और चौड़ी वाली देखिए, क्योंकि वो उतनी ही testable हैं। Plasma membrane — all cells. Ribosome — all cells. पूरे table में सिर्फ़ यही दो rows all cells कहती हैं। बाक़ी हर एक पर कोई पाबंदी है।

<curious>और इस पर रुकना ज़रूरी है। तेरह structures में से, ठीक दो सार्वभौमिक हैं। जो बिल्कुल वही shared minimum है जिससे हमने ये sub-topic शुरू किया — एक membrane और ribosomes. Table चुपचाप पहले section से सहमत है।
अब इसे पढ़ने के बजाय इस्तेमाल कैसे करें। इसे self-test की तरह इस्तेमाल कीजिए। दाईं column ढक दीजिए और organelle के नामों से उसे दोबारा बनाइए। फिर बाईं column ढक कर function से नाम की तरफ़ उल्टा चलिए।
वही दो-तरफ़ा drill matching सवाल माँगता है। वो आपको कभी वो दिशा नहीं देता जिसमें आपने अभ्यास किया हो। तो दोनों में अभ्यास कीजिए।

That list alone earns full marks. But a STRONG answer adds the one reverse fact...
...the ANIMAL cell uniquely keeps the CENTRIOLE — showing command of BOTH directions.

board_events.text: Answer: (a). The three double-membraned structures of the chapter. Exactly three — no more.
(b) Lysosome, Golgi, vacuole — all SINGLE-membraned. And all endomembrane members, which makes the set FEEL right.

board_events.text: 1. MIXING THE TWO FORKS. Prokaryote/eukaryote is about the NUCLEUS; plant/animal is about the wall, plastids, vacuole, centriole. Don't answer one fork's question with the other's facts.
2. RIBOSOME-SIZE REVERSAL. 70S = prokaryote + mitochondria/plastids. 80S = eukaryotic cytoplasm. The single most repeated trap in the chapter.
3. 'MEMBRANE-BOUND = ENDOMEMBRANE.' Mitochondria, chloroplasts and microbodies are membrane-bound yet excluded — membership needs COORDINATED FUNCTION.
4. CENTRIOLES IN PLANT CELLS / MITOCHONDRIA FOR ALL RESPIRATION. Higher plants lack centrioles; bacteria respire via the mesosome.
5. ADDING MEMBRANES TO INCLUSION BODIES OR THE NUCLEOID. Both are membrane-less. Only true organelles and the nucleus get membranes.
PRO-TIP: on any 'odd one out' or 'correctly grouped' question, sort the options by MEMBRANE COUNT (0 / 1 / 2) FIRST.

board_events.text: CELL THEORY: Schleiden + Schwann (cells and products of cells) + Virchow (cells from pre-existing cells). VIRUSES are the exception.
TWO FORKS: prokaryote vs eukaryote = is the DNA walled off? · plant vs animal = is the WHOLE CELL walled off?
PROKARYOTE: nucleoid (naked circular DNA + plasmids) · 70S ribosomes · peptidoglycan wall · mesosome · inclusion bodies (no membrane) · shapes = bacillus / coccus / vibrio / spirillum.
PLANT adds W-P-V: Wall (cellulose), Plastids, big Vacuole. ANIMAL keeps the centriole. Plant stores STARCH, animal stores GLYCOGEN.
MEMBRANE COUNT: 0 → ribosome, centriole, cytoskeleton, wall · 1 → ER, Golgi, lysosome, vacuole, microbody · 2 → mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus.
RIBOSOMES: 70S (prokaryote + mito/plastid) · 80S (eukaryotic cytoplasm). ENDOMEMBRANE SYSTEM: ER + Golgi + lysosome + vacuole (coordinated); mito / chloroplast / microbody excluded.
TWO ARRAYS: axoneme 9 + 2 (cilia/flagella) · centriole 9 + 0.
NUCLEUS: double envelope + pores · nucleolus (rRNA) · chromatin (DNA + histones) → chromosomes (centromere → meta / sub-meta / acro / telo; satellite = SAT).

segments.text: You have seen this before, in sub-topic two. We are coming back to it deliberately, because now it covers the whole chapter, and because the next few sections are going to lean on it hard.
Three rows. Zero, one, two. Sort every structure in this chapter by one number: how many membranes wrap it.
Zero: ribosome, centriole, cytoskeleton, cell wall. Four entries now.
One: E R, Golgi, lysosome, vacuole, microbody. Five entries, the crowded row, and unchanged since sub-topic two.
Two: mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus. Three entries.

<curious>Now compare this against the version you learned in sub-topic two, and notice what changed. The zero row has grown. Back then it was ribosome and centriole. Now the cytoskeleton and the cell wall have joined it — because you have since met both, and neither has a membrane.

And notice what did not change. Still only three structures are double-membraned. That number has not moved for the whole chapter. Mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus. It was three in sub-topic two and it is three now, with every organelle in.
<whisper>So learn this sort properly, because this single fact is about to do more work than any other thing you carry into the exam. The next four sections will show you exactly how much.
Four integrative worked examples now, and each one deliberately crosses sub-topic boundaries. That is the point of this sub-topic — the exam stops asking about one thing at a time.
First, a board question. List four features present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell. Four. And the mnemonic hands you three of them before you have finished reading the question.
Start from W-P-V. Cell wall, of cellulose. Plastids, including chloroplasts. A large central vacuole. Three down, one to go, and it took no thought at all.

<curious>So what is the fourth? You could reach for lysosomes, but remember the table said rare, not absent — so that is a risky answer. You could reach for shape, but that is not a feature, it is a consequence.

The fourth is plasmodesmata. And it is the natural fourth for a reason worth stating: it exists only because the wall does. No wall means no channels needed through the wall. So it belongs to the same cluster as W.
That list of four earns full marks. Wall, plastids, vacuole, plasmodesmata. Write it, and you have the question.
But there is a difference between a correct answer and a strong one, and this is where you separate yourself. A strong answer adds the one reverse fact.

<whisper>The animal cell uniquely keeps the centriole. One extra clause, and it shows command of both directions — not just what the plant adds, but what the animal held on to. The examiner asked one way. Answering both ways costs you eight words and demonstrates you understand the fork rather than just remembering a list.

A matching question, and notice how it is built. Four items, and every one comes from a different corner of the chapter. Nucleoid from sub-topic one. Eighty S from sub-topic two. Chitin from the master table. Inclusion bodies from sub-topic one again.
So there is no single page you can revise to answer this. That is the design. Use the technique instead: match the certainties first, and let the rest fall out.

A is the nucleoid, and it matches four: the prokaryotic D N A region. And notice that is almost a definition rather than a fact. The nucleoid is the region where prokaryotic D N A sits. Lock it in and move on.
B is the eighty S ribosome, and it matches two: eukaryotic cytoplasm. Hold that one lightly for a second, because the trap is built right here, and we will come back to it.

C is the chitin wall, and it matches one: fungal cell. And this is why you read the wall row of the master table carefully. Cellulose plants, chitin fungi, absent animals. If you have that row, C takes one second.

D is the inclusion body, and it matches three: a free, non-membranous store. Free, meaning lying loose in the cytoplasm. Non-membranous, meaning no membrane around it. Both halves of the clue point at the same structure.

<whisper>Now the trap, and it is the sharpest one in this sub-topic. Did you feel the pull to pair the eighty S with mitochondria? It is tempting, and here is why it works: mitochondria really do have ribosomes. That part is true. Your instinct is not wrong about the fact — it is wrong about the number.

Because those ribosomes run seventy S, not eighty S. The mitochondrion carries the prokaryotic ribosome, and that is precisely the semi-autonomy we spent a section on. So the true fact leads you to the wrong pairing. That is what a good distractor does — it uses something you know correctly to move you somewhere wrong.
This M C Q is a small piece of craftsmanship, and it is worth admiring before you answer it, because seeing how it was built is the lesson.
The question: which set is correctly grouped as double-membraned? Four sets of three organelles each. Twelve organelles from across the whole chapter.

The answer is (a): mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus. The three double-membraned structures of the chapter. Exactly three, no more. If you carried that row in, you were done before you read the other options.

But read them anyway, because there is something unusual going on. Option (b): lysosome, Golgi, vacuole. All single-membraned. Not a random collection — a perfectly coherent group. Every member has exactly one membrane.

And notice the extra layer of temptation in (b). All three are endomembrane members. So the set feels right. It feels like a group that belongs together, because it is. Just not for the reason the question asked about.

Option (c): ribosome, centriole, cell wall. All non-membranous. That is the zero row from the last section, offered to you intact. It is a correct group. It is the right answer to a different question.
Option (d): E R, microbody, plasma membrane. All single-membraned again. Another clean group.

<curious>Now see the design. Each wrong option is a clean membrane-count group — just not the one asked for. The examiner did not write sloppy distractors; they wrote three correct groups and asked you which count matches. And that is exactly what makes the zero-one-two recall decisive here. If you know the counts, this question takes four seconds. If you do not, all four options look equally defensible.
The last worked example of the chapter, and it is the one that best rewards having understood rather than memorised. It reaches back to sub-topic one to answer a question about sub-topic two.
Assertion: a bacterial cell can carry out aerobic respiration without possessing mitochondria. Reason: in prokaryotes, respiratory functions are associated with the mesosome and plasma membrane.

Test A on its own. Can a bacterium respire aerobically with no mitochondria? A is true. Many bacteria respire aerobically, and none of them has a mitochondrion. This is not a rare exception — it is how most of the living world does it.
Test R on its own. R is true as well. The mesosome, which you met in sub-topic one, is an infolding of the plasma membrane, and respiratory functions are indeed associated with it.
So both are true. And now the extra step: does R explain A? Yes, and this time the explanation is genuinely mechanical, not just a nearby fact.

Here is the reasoning. The mesosome takes on the respiratory and membrane-associated roles that organelles handle in eukaryotes. So the bacterium is not doing without respiration — it is doing without the organelle, by doing the same chemistry on a different surface. R names the surface. That is why R explains A.
So: both true, R explains A. Option (a).

<whisper>And now the trap, which is one of the most instructive in the chapter. The trap is assuming that no mitochondria equals no aerobic respiration. It feels airtight — you learned mitochondrion is the site of aerobic respiration, so no mitochondrion should mean no respiration. But look at what that assumption really does: it confuses a solution with a requirement. The mitochondrion is one solution to respiration, not the requirement for it. Eukaryotes built an organelle. Prokaryotes folded a membrane. Same chemistry, two architectures — which is fork one, all over again.

Five pitfalls for the whole chapter. And look at what unites them: not one is about content you failed to learn. Every one is about content you know, applied to the wrong fork, the wrong direction, or the wrong scale.
Look at the board. Five traps on the left, one small sort on the right. We will finish on the right-hand side, because it is worth more than the five put together.

Pitfall one: mixing the two forks. Prokaryote versus eukaryote is about the nucleus. Plant versus animal is about the wall, plastids, vacuole, centriole. So do not answer one fork's question with the other's facts. If someone asks what makes a cell eukaryotic and you say a cell wall, you have answered the wrong fork.

Pitfall two: ribosome-size reversal. Seventy S is prokaryote plus mitochondria and plastids. Eighty S is eukaryotic cytoplasm. This is the single most repeated trap in the chapter, and it has now shown up in three separate worked examples across three sub-topics. That is not an accident.

Pitfall three: membrane-bound equals endomembrane. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and microbodies are membrane-bound and yet excluded. Membership needs coordinated function. Counting membranes is the wrong test for that question — even though, as you are about to see, it is the right test for almost every other one.

Pitfall four is really two pitfalls with the same shape. Centrioles in plant cells: higher plants lack them. Mitochondria for all respiration: bacteria respire via the mesosome. Both are cases of taking a eukaryotic, or animal, default and assuming it is universal.

Pitfall five: adding membranes to inclusion bodies or the nucleoid. Both are membrane-less. Only true organelles and the nucleus get membranes. A prokaryote does not do membranes on the inside — that is the whole point of fork one.

<whisper>And now the pro-tip, which is the single most useful thing in this sub-topic. On any odd-one-out or correctly-grouped question, do not reason about function. Sort the options by membrane count — zero, one, two — first. A large fraction of chapter-spanning M C Qs collapse the moment you do, because the examiner almost always builds the distractors along that axis. You watched it happen in worked example three: four options, four clean membrane-count groups. Once you know where to look, the question tells you how it was made.

Cell theory. Schleiden and Schwann gave us cells and products of cells. Virchow gave us cells from pre-existing cells. And viruses are the exception — acellular, outside the theory.

Two forks. Prokaryote versus eukaryote: is the D N A walled off? Plant versus animal: is the whole cell walled off? One question, two scales. If you remember nothing else structural, remember this line.

Prokaryote. Nucleoid, holding naked circular D N A plus plasmids. Seventy S ribosomes. Peptidoglycan wall. Mesosome. Inclusion bodies, with no membrane. And the four shapes: bacillus, coccus, vibrio, spirillum.
Plant versus animal. The plant adds W-P-V: wall of cellulose, plastids, big vacuole. The animal keeps the centriole. And the storage pair: plant stores starch, animal stores glycogen.

Membrane count. Zero: ribosome, centriole, cytoskeleton, wall. One: E R, Golgi, lysosome, vacuole, microbody. Two: mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus. This is the line that does the most work in the exam hall.

Ribosomes: seventy S for prokaryote plus mitochondria and plastids; eighty S for eukaryotic cytoplasm. And the endomembrane system: E R plus Golgi plus lysosome plus vacuole, coordinated — with mitochondrion, chloroplast and microbody excluded.
Two arrays. Axoneme nine plus two, for cilia and flagella. Centriole nine plus zero. Two numbers, two addresses.

<excited>And the nucleus. Double envelope with pores. Nucleolus, making ribosomal R N A. Pitfall पाँच — inclusion bodies या nucleoid पर membranes चढ़ा देना। दोनों membrane-less हैं। सिर्फ़ true organelles और nucleus को membranes मिलती हैं। Prokaryote अंदर membranes करता ही नहीं — यही तो fork एक की पूरी बात है।

Chapter भर के M C Qs का बड़ा हिस्सा उसी पल ढह जाता है, क्योंकि examiner लगभग हमेशा distractors उसी धुरी पर बनाता है। आपने इसे worked example तीन में होते देखा — चार options, चार साफ़ membrane-count समूह। एक बार पता चल जाए कि कहाँ देखना है, तो सवाल ख़ुद बता देता है कि वो बना कैसे था।
ये chapter का आख़िरी section है, और यही वो है जिस पर लौटना है। सब कुछ, एक पन्ने पर निचोड़ा हुआ। Exam से एक रात पहले यही पढ़िए, और कुछ नहीं।
Board देखिए। नौ पट्टियाँ। हर पट्टी एक chapter है जिससे आप गुज़र चुके हैं, दो लाइनों में मुड़ा हुआ। यहाँ कुछ नया नहीं है — यही बात है। अगर कोई लाइन चौंकाए, वही sub-topic दोबारा खोलिए।
Cell theory. Schleiden और Schwann ने दिया — cells और cells के products. Virchow ने दिया — cells पहले से मौजूद cells से। और viruses अपवाद हैं — acellular, theory के बाहर।
दो forks. Prokaryote बनाम eukaryote — क्या D N A दीवार से अलग है? Plant बनाम animal — क्या पूरी cell दीवार से अलग है? एक सवाल, दो scales. अगर structural तौर पर कुछ और याद न रहे, ये लाइन याद रखिए।

Prokaryote. Nucleoid, जिसमें naked circular D N A plus plasmids. Seventy S ribosomes. Peptidoglycan wall. Mesosome. Inclusion bodies, बिना membrane. और चार shapes — bacillus, coccus, vibrio, spirillum.
Plant बनाम animal. Plant जोड़ता है W-P-V — cellulose की wall, plastids, बड़ा vacuole. Animal रखता है centriole. और storage की जोड़ी — plant starch store करता है, animal glycogen.

Membrane count. Zero — ribosome, centriole, cytoskeleton, wall. One — E R, Golgi, lysosome, vacuole, microbody. Two — mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus. यही वो लाइन है जो exam hall में सबसे ज़्यादा काम करती है।

Ribosomes — seventy S prokaryote plus mitochondria और plastids के लिए; eighty S eukaryotic cytoplasm के लिए। और endomembrane system — E R plus Golgi plus lysosome plus vacuole, coordinated — और mitochondrion, chloroplast तथा microbody बाहर।
दो arrays. Axoneme nine plus two, cilia और flagella के लिए। Centriole nine plus zero. दो numbers, दो पते।

<excited>और nucleus. Double envelope, pores के साथ। Nucleolus, ribosomal R N A बनाता हुआ। Chromatin, histones पर D N A, chromosomes में condense होता हुआ — centromere की स्थिति से metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric; satellite से S A T chromosome. और यही chapter है। अस्सी sections, चार sub-topics, एक पन्ना। आपने cytoplasm की एक थैली और एक membrane से शुरू किया था, और अब आप उसके अंदर की हर चीज़ जानते हैं। जाइए और इस्तेमाल कीजिए।
